A tercet is a group of exactly three lines in a poem, set together as a unit.

You already know what a stanza is — it's a group of lines in a poem that are clustered together and separated from the next group by a blank line, much like a paragraph in prose. A tercet is simply a stanza that contains three lines. That's the heart of it.

So if you see this in a poem:

The stars above the hill glow bright,
They pierce the cold and moonless night,
And fill the world with silver light.

...that is a tercet. Three lines, grouped together.

A tercet doesn't have to follow one fixed rhyme pattern. The three lines can rhyme with each other in several different ways. Here are the main ones:

  • AAA — All three lines rhyme with each other. (bright / night / light, as above.)
  • ABA — The first and third lines rhyme; the middle line does not.
  • ABB or AAB — Two of the lines rhyme; one doesn't.
  • ABC — No lines rhyme at all.

The crucial point here is: the rhyme pattern is flexible. What makes something a tercet is not the rhyme — it is purely the number three. Three lines, grouped together, make a tercet, rhyme or no rhyme.

When all three lines in a tercet rhyme with each other (the AAA pattern), the tercet earns a special name: a triplet. The example at the top of this page (bright / night / light) is a triplet.

The relationship between the two words is this:

  • Every triplet is a tercet (because it has three lines).
  • But not every tercet is a triplet (because a tercet's lines don't all have to rhyme).

A triplet is simply a specific type of tercet — the one where all three lines rhyme.
The Most Famous Use of Tercets: Terza Rima

The most celebrated use of tercets in all of literary history is a poetic form called terza rima, made famous by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri in his masterwork The Divine Comedy (early 14th century).

In terza rima, the poem is built from an unbroken chain of interlocking ABA tercets, like this:

First tercet: A B A
Second tercet: B C B
Third tercet: C D C
Fourth tercet: D E D
...and so on.

Look at how the middle line (B) of the first tercet becomes the outer rhyme sound (B) that brackets the second tercet. Then the middle line of the second tercet (C) becomes the outer rhyme of the third, and so on endlessly. The tercets are chained together like interlocking rings, so the poem never comes to a complete stop until the very final moment when the chain is deliberately closed.

This continuous forward motion — one tercet always reaching into the next — gives terza rima an incredible sense of momentum and inevitability, which is part of why Dante used it for a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. The English poet Percy Bysshe Shelley used this same form in his famous poem Ode to the West Wind (1820).
Tercets as Building Blocks Inside Larger Poems

A tercet doesn't only appear as a repeating stanza form throughout a poem. It can also appear as a component inside a larger, more complex poetic structure.

The clearest example is the Italian sonnet (also called the Petrarchan sonnet), a 14-line poem. Its final six lines — called the sestet — are often divided into two back-to-back tercets. So the poem's closing movement is constructed from two tercets working together to bring the poem to resolution.

In modern and contemporary poetry, poets frequently use tercets with no rhyme at all. Here, the three-line grouping becomes purely a visual and rhythmic choice — a way of controlling the pace at which the reader moves through the poem, and of packaging ideas into compact, equal-sized units. The poem may look neat and orderly on the page simply because every stanza is a tidy block of three lines, even if no two lines sound alike. Many modern poets favored this approach precisely because the structure provides a sense of form and discipline without forcing the content into a rhyme.
How a Tercet Compares to Other Stanza Types

All of the following are simply stanzas named after the number of lines they contain:

  • A couplet = 2 lines
  • A tercet = 3 lines
  • A quatrain = 4 lines
  • A quintet = 5 lines
  • A sestet = 6 lines
  • An octave = 8 lines

The tercet sits at "three." These names are just the vocabulary poets and literary scholars use to describe the shapes of stanzas.

Less commonly, the word "tercet" also appears in music, where it refers to a group of three notes played in the time that would normally be given to two — what musicians more commonly call a triplet. This is a minority usage. When most people say "tercet," they mean the three-line poetic unit described throughout this explanation.

A tercet is a group of exactly three lines in a poem. The three lines may rhyme in a variety of patterns (AAA, ABA, ABB, AAB) or may not rhyme at all. When all three lines rhyme, the tercet is specifically called a triplet. Tercets can appear as the sole repeating stanza form throughout a poem, or as components within a larger poetic structure (such as the closing sestet of an Italian sonnet). The most celebrated use of tercets is terza rima — a form of interlocking ABA tercets chained together in an unbroken sequence — made legendary by Dante. The tercet is one of the fundamental building blocks of poetry across cultures and centuries.
